abstract: | 
  Schools are key spaces of meritocratic socialization, shaping students' understanding of whether success is earned or inherited. Yet little is known about how students conceive meritocracy and how these conceptions relate to the acceptance of privilege. This study examines whether perceptions and preferences about meritocracy and privilege form distinct yet related dimensions of students' beliefs, and how they change over time and across school stages. Using a novel instrument previously applied to adults, we surveyed Chilean students in 6th and 9th grade (Wave 1: N = 846) and again in 7th and 10th grade (Wave 2: N = 662). Results support a multidimensional organization of beliefs that is equivalent across waves but only partially across school stages. Endorsing meritocracy did not imply rejecting privilege: about one third of students held both positions, although their latent association was weak and inconsistent across groups. Latent means did not change significantly over one year. Secondary students were more skeptical than primary students about whether effort is rewarded, a cross-sectional contrast limited by item non-equivalence. Students can thus separate these beliefs by early adolescence, whereby supporting meritocracy does not imply a rejection of privilege. The study contributes a conceptual and measurement perspective to the understanding of meritocratic and privilege beliefs in school-aged populations, and provides a foundation for future research on the developmental trajectory of these beliefs and their educational implications.
  
  \medskip
  
  **Keywords**: Meritocracy · Privilege · Schools · Measurement invariance · Socialization · Chile
